newsitem.title: UK: Dollar rangebound, focus on U.S. trade data, G7.
newsitem.headline: Dollar rangebound, focus on U.S. trade data, G7.

text.p: The dollar was broadly steady, with traders looking to U.S. trade figures later Thursday and the summit of the Group of Seven leading industrial nations starting Friday to trigger a breakout from its narrowing ranges.
A stronger-than-expected business survey from Germany's Ifo research institute weighed on the dollar, causing it to pare overnight gains.

Trade relations between the U.S. and Japan remained the focus, though, with traders looking for signs of friction between the two countries over a renewed widening in Japan's trade and current account surpluses.

"Things are very quiet and I'm not expecting much to happen before the trade report," said Harry Culham, a trader at Merrill Lynch. "People are pretty square going into the G7 but there is some Japanese trust interest to buy dollars on dips."
The dollar was at 1.7304/09 marks at 1030 GMT from 1.7320/30 late Wednesday in Europe. It was at 113.16/21 yen from 113.41/46 yesterday.

Economists expect the U.S. trade report at 1230 GMT to show the deficit widened to $10 billion in April from $8.5 billion in March. This comes a day after Japan reported a 93 percent year-on-year surge in its May trade surplus with the U.S..
Traders are expecting G7 leaders and finance ministers to comment on the issue when they gather in Denver tomorrow for their three-day summit.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said overnight they will discuss the risk that further significant increases in Japan's trade surpluses will undermine growth in other countries and trigger a backlash against trade liberalisation.

Officials from Japan's Economic Planning Agency and Ministry of International Trade and Industry said Thursday the rises in Japan's trade surplus were a temporary phenomenon. Analysts expect they will persist long enough to weaken the dollar.

"No-one wants to go short ahead of the G7 but given that Japan's trade surpluses will continue to rise in the next quarter or two, there will be downward pressure on dollar/yen," said Paul Megyessi, strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
The dollar is almost 12 percent below the four-and-a-half-year high of 127.46 yen it set on May 1, but is still more than 40 percent above the postwar low it set in April 1995.

In an indication that Japanese exporters are still competitive at current exchange rates, the chairman of the Japan Iron and Steel Federation, Takashi Imai, said Thursday a dollar/yen rate of 113 was a good level for Japan.

The dollar struggled to make headway against the mark after the Ifo institute said its West German business climate index rose to 95.3 in May from 94.7 in April while the region's business expectations index rose to 104.1 from 103.5.

"The German economy is recovering but it is still not very spectacular, said Lee Ferridge, the currency strategist at Commerzbank. "Over time people will begin to talk about the need for higher German rates, but until then, figures like these shouldn't have too much of a lasting impact."
At 5.5 percent, the target U.S. fed funds rate is 2.5 percentage points above the German securities repurchase rate.

U.S. interest-rate premiums and expectations that a broad group of European Union countries, including Italy, will launch the economic and monetary union in 1999 are seen underpinning dollar/mark in the coming weeks.

"The long-term players are still looking to buy dollars against the Europeans on the weak euro argument," said Austin White, the manager of foreign exchange at Yamaichi. -Swaha Pattanaik, London newsroom +44 171 542 6284
